summary: This video documents a practical post-processing workflow for abstract Desert drone imagery, focusing on building a strong big-to-small compositional transition that leads the viewer toward the light source. The presenter demonstrates global RAW adjustments (shadows, blacks, whites, and exposure) to recover depth, then refines color balance with temperature and tint. A recurrent theme is controlled, large-brush editing over small brush work, aided by the History Brush to selectively apply adjustments. The session covers both RAW/Camera Raw and Photoshop workflows for localized edits, plus specific color tools (de-haze, blue-gold filter, color grading, and selective color) to heighten depth and mood. The tutorial also delves into advanced techniques for panoramas: stitching with PTGui (rectilinear vs other projections, handling multiple exposures, and TIFF output), then importing into Photoshop for final crops and light-direction adjustments. Throughout, the emphasis is on guiding the eye along light, texture, and transitions to create cohesive, multi-layered abstracts and landscape-based compositions.

sections.title: Global RAW pass and color balance
concepts: Camera Raw color balance (temperature and tint)
sections.description: Begin with a global RAW pass to reveal color and depth. The instructor emphasizes pulling out shadows and blacks, reducing exposure, and using whites to recover color, followed by adjusting color temperature and tint for a natural look.

sections.title: Targeted light flow and localized adjustments
concepts: Guiding the eye toward the light source
sections.description: After the initial global pass, the presenter demonstrates targeted adjustments to draw the eye upward toward the light source. This includes using a localized approach and painting selective changes with the History Brush at reduced opacity.

sections.title: Refining light, depth, and brush strategy
concepts: Adding more light and softer haze
sections.description: The workflow adds more light from the upper part of the frame, softens the look to imply distance, and emphasizes a big-to-small transition. The speaker cautions against using many tiny brushes and advocates larger brushes for efficiency and consistency.

sections.title: Two-pass whites adjustments and vignette planning
concepts: Masking to keep whites from blowing out
Creating a vignette to guide eye to the focal area
sections.description: Two separate whites-based adjustments are used to manage extreme highlights in bright regions. The second pass involves masking and selective painting back into the shot to preserve color consistency, followed by a vignette to direct attention toward the light source. Color balance is tweaked to keep overall color believable.

sections.title: Panorama stitching with PTGui and initial Photoshop prep
concepts: Export as TIFF or DNG for uncompressed quality
Import into Photoshop and crop for composition
sections.description: The section focuses on assembling a multi-image panorama with PTGui, choosing the appropriate projection, and dealing with different exposure levels across images. Output is saved as TIFF for later Photoshop processing, where cropping tightens the composition to emphasize leading lines and horizon flow.

sections.title: Final color grading and simulated light in panoramas
concepts: Simulated light source and glow effects
Foreground/background separation with selective color and gradient tools
Edge handling and vignette for depth
Lucy-level adjustments: dodge/burn, de-haze, and saturation control
sections.description: In the later segment, the focus shifts to panoramic color grading, with emphasis on simulating light sources, adding glow, and balancing foreground and background. The instructor demonstrates selective color and gradient adjustments, dodge/burn, de-haze, and careful edge handling to maintain cohesive depth and visual flow.
